Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. Title: Diagnosis
Details: 

The test `testContainsAnyStringWithSupplementaryChars()` fails because `StringUtils.containsAny` does not correctly handle Unicode supplementary characters, i.e., characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP) which are represented in Java as surrogate pairs (two char values).

In detail, the test uses supplementary characters U+20000 and U+20001 which are represented as surrogate pairs: `"\uD840\uDC00"` and `"\uD840\uDC01"` respectively. These characters are 2-char sequences in Java, not a single char.

Inspecting the `StringUtils.containsAny` method's code shows the root cause:

- The method `containsAny(CharSequence cs, String searchChars)` converts `searchChars` to a char array and calls `containsAny(CharSequence cs, char[] searchChars)`.
- The method `containsAny(CharSequence cs, char[] searchChars)` then iterates over each single `char` in `cs` and checks if it matches any of the `searchChars` (also individual chars).
- This approach inherently treats each element as a single 16-bit char, thus failing for supplementary characters which require surrogate pairs (two `char`).

Because `containsAny` does not account for surrogate pairs, it cannot correctly match supplementary characters that are represented as two `char` values in Java strings. It compares `char` values directly, leading to incorrect matching behavior for Unicode 2.0+ supplementary characters.

Hence, the fundamental cause is that the current implementation uses `char` unit comparison, ignoring that supplementary characters are represented as pairs of UTF-16 code units in Java. The method needs to be updated to handle supplementary characters correctly through code points rather than just chars.

This matches the bug report summary and test nature exactly: failure of `containsAny` on supplementary Unicode characters.

Next, further investigation can explore whether other related `StringUtils` methods have the same issue and identify how to fix it by switching to code point iteration rather than char iteration.
org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils.containsAny(java.lang.CharSequence, char[])
org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils.containsAny(java.lang.CharSequence, java.lang.String)
